stories.headline: Trump, Xi and Putin set for first trilateral summit in Shenzhen

sources.body:
"We'll have a second meeting later on as you probably know, but we'll have this right now and it'll be great," Trump says, before he shakes hands with Putin again.

As we have been reporting, Trump and Putin are due to hold a trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping later today.

The footage ends with the two leaders taking their seats. Typically, at such meetings, the press is not allowed to cover the rest of the discussions, but either the US or Russia may later release a summary of what was discussed.
sources.headline: Trump, Xi and Putin set to hold historic meeting on Apec sidelines

sources.body: The leaders of China, the US and Russia are set to hold a first-of-its-kind trilateral meeting on Thursday in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of an APEC summit. The meeting between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, which Beijing said would involve "safeguarding world peace", has raised fears of a carve-up of the globe into "spheres of influence". Follow our liveblog for the latest developments.
sources.headline: Xi-Trump-Putin talks live: China, US and Russia leaders to hold landmark three-way meeting

sources.body:
The US, Chinese and Russian leaders are to hold their first three-way talks on the sidelines of the APEC summit.

US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin will hold a three-way meeting on Thursday in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, the first ever between the leaders of the world’s three most powerful militaries.

The meeting, which will take place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, has drawn comparisons with the 1945 wartime Yalta conference at which the United States, United Kingdom and then-Soviet Union agreed on the post-war order. But those powers had been allied during a world war. Analysts say the three men meeting on Thursday are arriving with very different goals, and that few concrete outcomes can be expected.

“It’s a summit of Trump’s ego, Putin’s tactics, China’s strategy,” Scott Lucas, professor of international politics at University College Dublin, told Al Jazeera.

So what does each leader want from this meeting?

The trilateral meeting is taking place on the sidelines of the APEC leaders’ summit, which China is hosting in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19. Trump travelled to China after attending the Association of Southeast Asian Nations ( ASEAN ) meeting in Manila.

The White House has said that Trump plans to discuss the war with Iran as well as a possible three-way agreement on nuclear armament with Xi and Putin. Ukraine is not expected to be on the formal agenda, as Xi is understood to be reluctant to be drawn into what he views as a European matter.

The meeting comes as Trump has strained ties with traditional US allies, at times floating troop withdrawals from South Korea and cuts to assistance for Japan, while his administration continues to describe China as Washington’s main geopolitical rival.

Vuk Vuksanovic, a lecturer in foreign policy and grand strategy at the Department of War Studies, King’s College, London, cautioned against viewing the summit as a new “carve-up” of the world order, however.

“It is a far cry from being a new Yalta,” he said. “In Yalta, you actually had the idea about how the world was going to look, and where the demarcation line would potentially be between the superpowers. We don’t have anything similar, not even the contours of that, in the making at this moment.”

At the Yalta Conference in February 1945, US President Franklin D Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met in Crimea to shape the post-war order, agreeing on the division of Germany and setting the stage for Soviet influence over Eastern Europe.

There are competing interests at play here.

Trump landed in Shenzhen on Wednesday, with Xi greeting him at the airport. This is their third in-person meeting since they paused their bitter trade war late last year. At its height, US trade tariffs on Chinese goods reached 145 percent, with China retaliating with tariffs of 125 percent on US goods, before a temporary truce agreed in Busan, South Korea, in October 2025, when tariffs were relaxed. Xi also agreed to pause new restrictions on exports of some rare earth metals which are crucial for manufacturing technology from smartphones to fighter jets. Soon after that, Trump relaxed restrictions on the sale of some Nvidia AI-related computer chips to China.
sources.headline: What do Trump, Putin and Xi want from their Shenzhen meeting?

stories.headline: Myanmar faces landmark UN court ruling over Rohingya genocide allegations

sources.body:
When the judges of the International Court of Justice read out their verdict in the seven-year-old genocide case filed by The Gambia against Myanmar on Thursday, they could make history.

In the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in 1948, after the Nazi Holocaust, dozens of individuals have been successfully prosecuted for the crime of genocide, in conflicts such as those in Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia.

But no state has ever been found guilty by an international court of committing genocide.

"It would be a judgment of landmark importance if The Gambia were to win this case," says Arsalan Suleman, the lawyer leading the case against Myanmar at the court. "It would give renewed vitality to the 1948 Genocide Convention and to the notion of international legal accountability for crimes committed by a state."

The mass expulsion of the Rohingya population of Rakhine State in August and September 2017 was without question a military operation of exceptional brutality.

I was among a very small number of journalists who witnessed the deliberate burning of Rohingya villages in Rakhine, and also the dreadful human suffering of the hundreds of thousands who fled to neighbouring Bangladesh.

Their accounts of killing, torture and mass rape by Burmese soldiers have been thoroughly documented by human rights groups and a United Nations fact-finding mission .

I have on many occasions interviewed ethnic Rakhine people about their animosity towards the Muslim population, and I have documented the systematic obliteration of what remained of Rohingya villages by the Myanmar state.

But the question posed at the UN's top court, the ICJ, is whether all of this amounted to genocide.

The ICJ was established in 1945 to help settle disputes between states, not to try international crimes. However, it was chosen to address the attacks on Rohingyas in Myanmar because there were few other avenues of redress for the victims.

Myanmar authorities have denied accusations of ethnic cleansing or genocide, saying they were only responding to terrorist actions by Rohingya militants with so-called military "clearance operations".

A UN report in 2018 , based on hundreds of interviews, said the army's tactics were "grossly disproportionate to actual security threats". It said top military figures in Myanmar must be investigated for genocide in Rakhine State and crimes against humanity in other areas. Myanmar rejected the report.

As Myanmar was not a signatory to the International Criminal Court, it was not possible to file a case there against the officials accused of atrocities in Rakhine State.

Instead in November 2019 The Gambia, backed by the Organisation of Islamic Co-operation, filed a case at the ICJ, arguing that all states are bound by the Genocide Convention, so all have an interest in upholding it.

It accused the state in Myanmar, not just the military, of genocide.

This was a novelty in international law; a state not directly affected by an act, arguing that it had legal standing to make a complaint because it was indirectly affected by any violations of such an important convention.
sources.headline: Myanmar faces historic genocide verdict at UN court over Rohingya massacres

sources.body:
The Gambia accused Myanmar of genocide following a 2017 military crackdown displacing over 730,000 Rohingya.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ), the United Nations’ highest court, is set to rule in a landmark case accusing Myanmar of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority.

The reading of the judgment will begin at 10am (09:00 GMT) on Thursday at the Peace Palace in The Hague and is expected to last up to 90 minutes.

It could be the first time the court rules that a state has committed genocide.

The ruling is final and cannot be appealed, but the court has very limited means of enforcing it. If Myanmar ignores it, The Gambia could ask the UN Security Council to act.

The Gambia, a Muslim-majority West African country, brought the case in November 2019 with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.

It argues that Myanmar bears state responsibility for genocide resulting from a 2017 military offensive that drove at least 730,000 Rohingya, who are mostly Muslim, from Buddhist-majority Myanmar into Bangladesh.

Survivors have recounted killings, mass rape and the burning of villages. A UN fact-finding mission concluded that the campaign included “genocidal acts”.

Myanmar denies genocide and says its forces responded legitimately to attacks by armed groups. It argues there is no direct evidence of an intent to destroy the Rohingya.

Under the 1948 Genocide Convention, genocide requires proof of the specific intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.

The ICJ has never held a state responsible for committing genocide. In 2007, it found that Serbia had failed to prevent the 1995 Srebrenica massacre in Bosnia, in which more than 8,000 Muslim men and boys were killed, but ruled that Serbia had not itself committed genocide.

The judgment could also set precedents for other cases, including South Africa’s case accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza.

The ICJ settles disputes between states, so it can find Myanmar responsible but cannot try individuals, which is the duty of the International Criminal Court.

The Gambia has asked the ICJ to order Myanmar to prosecute those responsible, make reparations and ensure the Rohingya can return safely . Myanmar disputes The Gambia’s right to seek reparations on their behalf.

About 1.2 million Rohingya live in the Cox’s Bazar refugee settlement in Bangladesh, where many will follow the judgment, the Reuters news agency reported. Roughly 550,000 remain in Myanmar, with restrictions on their movement, healthcare and livelihoods.
sources.headline: ICJ to rule on Rohingya genocide case against Myanmar

stories.headline: Israeli tanks cross Gaza’s ceasefire boundary, forcing Palestinians to flee

sources.body:
First incursion across boundary since ceasefire deal comes as Eisenkot seeks to form government without Netanyahu

The Israeli military crossed into Hamas-controlled central Gaza on Wednesday in its first ground operation across the “yellow line” boundary since a fragile ceasefire was agreed last October, forcing dozens of displaced Palestinians to flee their tents.

Israeli tanks rolled along the Salah al-Din road , Gaza’s main north-south route, a day after the US-backed Board of Peace, a body overseeing the ceasefire, accused Israel and Hamas of failing to honour their commitments to end hostilities.

An Israeli military spokesperson said troops were carrying out an operation targeting “Hamas infrastructure” west of the yellow line in central Gaza .

The military ​has not commented extensively on the operation, which came as the Israeli opposition politician, Gadi Eisenkot, has been seeking to form a government without the caretaker prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, who has built his political reputation on promises to keep Israel safe.

A Gaza security source told AFP there was “intense Israeli artillery shelling” north of Nuseirat refugee camp and reported Israeli military vehicles in central Gaza “amid ongoing gunfire and airstrikes since midday”.

Hamas condemned the Israeli raid and the forced displacement of Palestinians as “a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement” and a dangerous escalation. The Israeli military did not immediately respond to Hamas’s statement.

Residents reported hearing tank fire in the area. Palestinian medics said one person was killed in an Israeli airstrike near the site of the raid.

In separate incidents on Wednesday, Palestinian medics said two people were killed by Israeli fire, one in Deir al-Balah and the other in Gaza City. The Israeli military said it was unaware of any incident in Deir al-Balah and had struck a militant in Gaza City.

Israel has stepped up its attacks on Hamas, which it says has been regrouping and rearming. Hamas has accused Israel of trying to derail the US-brokered ceasefire agreed in October 2025.

Israeli strikes have continued since the ceasefire, and Hamas remains armed.

Last week, an Israeli airstrike on Nasser hospital in southern Gaza killed six people, including a surgeon and a disabled man, and wounded 28 others, according to the hospital director.

The body overseeing Donald Trump’s plan to end the war in Gaza has accused Israel and Hamas of failing to honour their commitments to end hostilities, leaving Palestinians in dire conditions and the ceasefire at risk of collapse.

In its second report to the UN security council since the truce began 13 months ago, the Trump-led Board of Peace said the gap between what was agreed and what was happening on the ground remained the biggest threat to the deal. The report, seen by Reuters, warned that “a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely”.

Gaza’s health authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire came into effect. The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.
sources.headline: Israeli tanks cross ‘yellow line’ boundary into Hamas-controlled central Gaza

sources.body: Palestinians fled their tents and shelters in central Gaza on Wednesday after Israel launched a rare ground operation in an area it withdrew ​from under a ‌2025 ceasefire. The Israeli army said it crossed the Yellow Line separating Israeli and Hamas-controlled areas "to remove a threat posed to IDF troops operating in the Gaza Strip".
sources.headline: Gazans flee shelters as Israeli army launches ground operation beyond Yellow Line

sources.body:
Israeli ground forces have launched a rare operation in part of the central Gaza Strip outside their control, after issuing evacuation orders for residents.

Witnesses said tanks advanced east of Nuseirat refugee camp and rolled onto the territory's main north to south road under the cover of artillery strikes.

The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.

The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire agreement.

Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.

Early on Wednesday afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the incursion and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety.

It also said a section of the north to south Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.

Later, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had begun a joint operation with the Shin Bet security service "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".

"IDF troops under the Southern Command are deployed in the area in accordance with the ceasefire agreement and will continue to operate to remove any immediate threat and thwart attempts by the Hamas terrorist organisation to harm Israeli civilians or IDF troops, or to violate the agreement," it added.

Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement".

Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the announcement.

In one video verified by BBC Verify, a man can be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he says.

Automatic gunfire can be heard in another video filmed just to the south-east.

A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter."

"We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind."

A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and said there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities".

Asked about reported fatalities, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation.

Gaza's Hamas-run Civil Defence agency said three people were killed and others were wounded in three separate Israeli drone strikes on Wednesday.
sources.headline: Israeli military launches rare ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line

stories.headline: Saudi-led coalition strikes Houthi targets as rebels advance toward Aden

sources.body:
Houthis advance towards Aden as Saudi-led coalition conducts precision strikes on key military targets in Yemen.

Yemen’s Houthis push closer to Aden as government forces reposition

Saudi-led coalition forces have carried out a “precision operation” in Yemen against 60 Houthi military targets and destroyed tunnels used by the armed group as workshops and storage for ballistic missiles, according to the coalition’s spokesman.

Turki al-Maliki said on Wednesday morning that the strikes came in the governorates of Sanaa, Hodeidah, Amran and Saada on Tuesday during an advance by the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), towards the southern city of Aden, the temporary capital of Yemen’s internationally recognised government.

In recent days, the Yemeni army and forces loyal to it withdrew from Dhubab airport and territory around the Bab-al-Mandeb strait, the strategic maritime chokepoint in western Taiz governorate, to defend Aden.

Elsewhere in Yemen, fighting resumed between the government forces and the Houthis in Tur al-Bahah in Lahij province.

Al Jazeera’s Hadeel al-Yamani, who is in Taiz, said “on the ground, fierce battles have been taking place between government forces and the Houthi group”.

“Local authorities accuse the Houthi group of shelling civilians and residential neighbourhoods,” al-Yamani said.

“These villages in Jabal Sabr are under a complete siege. There are urgent appeals for safe corridors to be opened for civilians, and daily sniper attacks [are] targeting civilians. People are being killed and injured, primarily children and women,” al-Yamani added.

Taiz authorities accused Houthis of establishing checkpoints to impose levies on civilians and confiscating shipments of medicines and medical supplies that lacked licences from Yemen’s Houthi-controlled capital, Sanaa.

In a statement published on Monday, Taiz’s Public Health and Population Office condemned the Houthis, saying “this escalatory move constitutes a direct assault on pharmaceutical security and a violation of the human right to access medicine and medical treatment”.

Taiz officials called on the United Nations to intervene, adding that Houthis were blocking the entry of medical supplies coming from Aden to Taiz, intensifying the ongoing siege and endangering “the lives of thousands of patients whose continued treatment” is at risk.

Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted two cruise missiles launched by Houthis towards the capital, Riyadh, on Wednesday. The attacks are the latest in weeks of strikes by the Yemeni armed group targeting Saudi military, civilian and oil infrastructure.

The Houthis’ military spokesman, Yahya Saree, said the group targeted oil pumping stations near Riyadh and a radar installation in southern Saudi Arabia.

Saudi authorities have so far not responded to the claims.

Alerts were sounded in the Saudi cities of Jizan, Najran and Khamis Mushait on Wednesday before the danger passed.
sources.headline: Saudi coalition hits 60 Houthi military sites; Taiz sees ‘fierce battles’

sources.body: Bolstered by their recent military successes, Houthi rebels this week advanced close to the southern port city of Aden, the interim capital of the internationally recognised Yemeni government. Amid territorial ambitions, regional rivalries, and divisions within government forces, the potential fall of this stronghold could permanently alter the balance of power in the country.
sources.headline: Yemen: Why the Houthis may besiege Aden rather than storm it

stories.headline: Hegseth visits Venezuela and announces renewed US military cooperation

sources.body: US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth made an unannounced visit to Caracas on Wednesday, announcing a resumption of military cooperation with Venezuela and vowing to crack down on drug traffickers. The trip marks the highest-level US visit since the ouster of Nicolas Maduro in January, signalling a dramatic shift in relations between the two countries.
sources.headline: Hegseth makes surprise trip to Venezuela, renews military cooperation

sources.body:
Defense secretary asserts US dominance on trip that would have seemed ‘impossible, almost unbelievable’ a year ago

Pete Hegseth has used his first visit to Venezuela since US special forces abducted its former president, Nicolás Maduro , to boast of the dictator’s capture during what he called “the single most sophisticated military operation in the history of Latin America”.

Maduro was controversially seized by Delta Force operatives in the early hours of 3 January, setting in motion an improbable rapprochement between Washington and Venezuela’s anti-imperialist “Chavista” regime, which has ruled since 1999.

Speaking outside the recently reopened US embassy in Venezuela’s capital, Caracas, on Wednesday, Hegseth said: “It’s a great honor to be here as the first United States secretary of war this century to set foot in Venezuela.​ Just one year ago my presence here … would have been deemed impossible, almost unimaginable.

“In fact, exactly one year ago today … [Maduro] stood on a stage not too far from here and yelled mockingly, ‘Come and get me!’” Hegseth recalled, before adding sarcastically: “Well, we answered that call.

“The reality is that … January 3 is the day that will go down in history as a day of liberation for Venezuela,” Hegseth claimed, although Maduro’s allies continue to hold power with US support.

Earlier in the day, Hegseth was welcomed to the Miraflores Palace by Maduro’s former vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez , who became acting president with Donald Trump’s blessing after his abduction.

In the aftermath of the deadly US attack, Hegseth was one of the bluntest Trump administration voices when it came to celebrating the invasion. “Maduro had his chance … he effed around and he found out,” the defense secretary bragged .

Speaking at the palace, Hegseth struck a more conciliatory tone as he vowed to deepen cooperation with Venezuela’s new leaders in brief comments that were broadcast by the state broadcaster VTV.

“I stand here on behalf of President Trump, who sends his greeting and looks forward to the opportunities, not just militarily … but also economically: the incredible resource capabilities that your country has, that we look forward to unlocking together with you,” Hegseth told Rodríguez and senior cabinet members, including the defense and foreign ministers, Gustavo González López and Oliver Blanco.

Hegseth said his visit to Rodríguez’s “beautiful country” was designed to re-establish and increase “defense cooperation” between “two great militaries” that less than a year ago were briefly at war. Earlier this month, the New York Times reported that Trump officials were trying to negotiate a long-term US troop presence in Venezuela as part of their push for regional hegemony.

“I appreciate your leadership and commitment to your country,” Hegseth told Maduro’s successor, a once outspoken anti-imperialist leftist who has overseen an unlikely realignment with Washington since her ally was grabbed.

During her five-minute address, Rodríguez, whose oil-rich country is widely seen to have become a US protectorate after January’s invasion, made no mention of Maduro, who is behind bars in New York City.
sources.headline: Hegseth uses Venezuela visit to boast of Maduro’s capture by US military

stories.headline: One in four women globally cannot refuse sex within marriage, UN reports

sources.body:
Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds

One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.

In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund ( UNFPA ) published on Thursday.

Younger women and girls aged 15 to 19 had even less power to say no, compared with older women aged 45 to 49, according to analysis in the report of eight countries with comparable data (Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kazakhstan, Malawi, Mali, Nigeria, Tajikistan and Zambia). The findings align with research showing adolescent girls endure very high rates of intimate partner violence.

“These are really sad figures,” said Jean-Paul Murunga, a lawyer with the global human rights organisation Equality Now. “Especially given that the continent of Africa as a whole has adopted the Maputo protocol, which sets [binding legal standards for] equality between women and men. We still have a lot of work to do to ensure women and girls benefit from these commitments.”

The Maputo protocol, a landmark treaty adopted by the African Union in 2003, guarantees women’s rights and obliges states to protect women from violence. It affirms that marriage must be based on full consent and guarantees women’s right to health.

“The underlying principle is unambiguous: sexual intercourse without free and voluntary consent constitutes sexual violence, including within marriage,” said Murunga. “Marriage does not create perpetual or implied consent. A woman retains the right to decide whether, when and how she engages in sexual activity”.

He said that as a first step rape laws across the continent needed to change. According to Murunga’s 2024 report, rape within marriage is not criminalised in some African countries. Seven countries expressly exempt husbands from prosecution for marital rape, including Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia and South Sudan. Some countries, such as Tanzania and Eritrea, only criminalise marital rape when the couple do not live together.

In countries where child marriage is permitted and marital rape is not criminalised, children are left unprotected. A legal loophole is created for what, outside marriage, would be classed as rape, and young wives have few options when it comes to protecting themselves from sexual violence and exploitation. In Gabon, for example, when a man has married a child he abducted , he can only be prosecuted after the marriage is annulled.

Underpinning these laws is the mistaken belief that marital rape does not exist as a concept because, by marrying, wives are assumed to have permanently consented to sex with their husbands. In many areas, religion plays a key role in affirming these beliefs.
sources.headline: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN

stories.headline: Anthropic’s record IPO tests investor appetite for AI

sources.body:
AI giant prices shares at $83 in blockbuster market debut.

Anthropic has raised $81.3bn in the largest initial public offering (IPO) in history, leapfrogging SpaceX’s initial $75bn market debut in June.

The San Francisco-based AI giant said in a statement late on Wednesday that the company and its seven co-founders had sold 980 million shares at $83 each.

The bigger-than-expected IPO comes after investor demand for the stock far outstripped forecasts.

Anthropic had said in corporate filings last week that it intended to offer 825 million shares at between $70 and $78 apiece.

The Claude creator is also set to raise $26bn through a private placement, a type of deal involving the sale of stock to private investors, taking the total capital raised to $107.3bn.

SpaceX’s total IPO haul later came to $85.7bn, after the deal’s underwriters exercised an overallotment option to purchase additional shares.

The blockbuster offering gives Anthropic a market value of roughly $1.5 trillion, making it the world’s 12th-biggest firm at current valuations, just behind Tesla.

Anthropic shares will begin trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange in New York on Thursday under the ticker “ANT”.

The public listing of Anthropic, founded in 2021 by former researchers from rival AI firm OpenAI, has been closely watched as a test of the eye-watering valuations of tech companies leading the AI rollout.

Tech firms have poured trillions of dollars into AI, expecting it to usher in revolutionary changes in business and society.

AI-related spending is forecast to reach $2.7 trillion in 2026 and $3.6 trillion in 2027, according to technology insights company Gartner.

Companies betting on the frontier technology currently make up roughly half of the value of the S&P 500 index.

The spending frenzy has stoked debate over whether Big Tech is funding a future gold mine or a speculative bubble like the one that preceded the 2000 dot-com crash.

Anthropic’s listing also comes as the market for the advanced graphics processing units that power AI is under a cloud amid the spying claims roiling chip giant Nvidia.

Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang stepped down last week amid unproven claims that a woman he was romantically involved with worked with the Chinese intelligence services.

The scandal has fuelled calls in the United States for stronger restrictions on China’s access to high-end chips, casting a pall over an AI boom partly sustained by Chinese developers’ remote access to data centres in Southeast Asia.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite stock index has shed nearly 7.6 percent of its value over the past month, led by a more than 30 percent plunge in Nvidia’s stock price.

Asian stock markets with heavy exposure to AI fell on Thursday despite the flurry of excitement around Anthropic, with South Korea’s Kospi, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index and Taiwan’s Taiex all in the red in morning trading.

Jay R Ritter, an IPO expert at the University of Florida, said that Anthropic’s ability to make profits to justify its valuation will depend on various factors, some of which are outside its control.
sources.headline: Anthropic raises $81.3bn in biggest IPO of all time

sources.body:
It was during November 2020 that somewhere in San Francisco, a woman called Daniela Amodei phoned a friend, asking for advice.

Daniela oversaw safety and policy at OpenAI, one of the most talked-about AI companies in the world.

But Daniela and her brother Dario - who worked there too - had misgivings over safety levels at OpenAI and thought it could be time to walk away.

So she did what many do when we can't make a decision about something, she phoned a friend. The friend's reply was direct and to the point: "You don't need to be on the phone with me. You already know the answer."

The Amodei siblings and a handful of other colleagues quit. Together, they set up a rival – Anthropic.

Six years on and Anthropic, the maker of leading AI model Claude, has predicted revenues of $52bn in 2026 and $135bn in 2027, according to analyst estimates.

It is about to sell shares to the public for the first time in what's known as an Initial Public Offering or IPO, aiming for a valuation of an estimated $1.4tn (£1tn), which would propel it straight into the top 10 of the most valuable US companies.

The sale comes at a crucial time when many are wondering whether, amid increasing concern about the potential of AI, the industry's bubble is showing signs of bursting.

Where once investors were "all in" on a technological revolution to rival the railroads, the car, electricity and the internet, some are now hedging their bets, amid arguments that AI prices will be driven down as the technology becomes more common and concerns that a hefty wedge of the AI investment is tech giants investing in each other.

Shares in companies that supply the raw computing power behind AI, like Coreweave and Nebius, have seen their value cut in half while even the mighty Nvidia has lost its crown as the world's most valuable company with its shares down 30% - a staggering $2tn fall in value.

So could the Anthropic IPO reinflate the bubble or will it be remembered as the last gasp of a boom that is heading for a bust?

At an event last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told JPMorgan Chase's CEO Jamie Dimon that his guiding principle was to "never let your company be worth a single dollar more than it's worth".

The company is selling roughly $65bn worth of shares to the general public and a further $26bn on to other big tech companies. It is comfortably the single biggest money raising event in US corporate history.

It's an old adage that during a gold rush you should buy companies that sell the picks and shovels as opposed to those staking everything on striking gold. In AI's case that's the chip makers, the data centre builders, the energy providers. But Anthropic is arguably the gold itself and this IPO will see what value people put on it, according to Fiona Cincotta.

"I think the reason that this IPO is so important is basically it's the first ability for the public investors to access a pure play AI trade," she says, adding that previous offerings have been about "other parts of the ecosystem, which are, the semiconductors, the chips, the, data centres. But this is the first time that we were actually able to access the AI provider."
sources.headline: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?

La empresa de Dario Amodei sale a bolsa con una fuerte demanda entre los inversores

Michael Nagle / Bloomberg L.P. Limited Partnership

Este es un momento en que se expande la paranoia por Estados Unidos ante los reiterados fallos tecnológicos y de los sistemas de computación.

Todas estas circunstancias, que han afectado a las comunicaciones por internet, el espacio aéreo, los bancos e incluso al espionaje de EE.UU. y que según la Administración Trump no se deben a ciberataques, se producen en medio de un creciente temor a la expansión de la inteligencia artificial, algo alentado por las advertencias de Dario Amodei, director ejecutivo de Anthropic. Pese a esas alertas de un posible fin del mundo por la IA, los inversores parece que se abrazan al apocalipsis al mostrar un interés enorme en la salida a bolsa de, precisamente, esa empresa que ha hecho sonar las alarmas de peligro.

Anthropic debutará hoy jueves en Wall Street, en una operación más que esperada.

Cotizará en el Nasdaq con el símbolo ANT y su precio de inicio se fijó en 83 dólares la acción, en una de las mayores salidas a bolsa de la historia. Esta cifra situaría su valoración en torno a 1,6 billones de dólares. Supone un incremento notable frente a los 1,33 billones de la horquilla inicial, cuando el precio de la acción se establecía entre 70 y 78 dólares.

Este importe superior al establecido inicialmente se debe a la fuerte demanda de los inversores. Ese incremento pone de manifiesto que las turbulencias del mercado y los problemas que atraviesa Nvidia no han mermado el entusiasmo por las inversiones vinculadas a la IA.

Si la salida a bolsa de Anthropic sigue adelante según lo previsto, la compañía debutará en el mercado aproximadamente cinco meses después de que SpaceX protagonizara una salida récord, con la que captó 85.700 millones de dólares. Anthropic captará de entrada unos 94.500 que podrían alcanzar los 1,6 billones con la sobreadjudicación.

Sin embargo, y al margen del apetito inicial, Anthropic se enfrenta a un mercado bursátil cada vez más escéptico respecto a las inversiones en inteligencia artificial, así como a una creciente y generalizada animadversión hacia esta tecnología en EE.UU., explicitada en el rechazo a los centros de datos.

Un grupo de investigadores, entre ellos Amodei, cofundó la empresa en el 2021, después de abandonar OpenAI, que ahora es su principal rival. Anthropic es conocida sobre todo por desarrollar una familia de modelos de inteligencia artificial llamada Claude. En el 2026 experimentó un periodo de crecimiento explosivo, impulsado en gran medida por la popularidad de su herramienta de programación con IA, Claude Code.

En los nueve meses transcurridos hasta el 30 de septiembre, la empresa declaró unos ingresos de 33.240 millones de dólares, un 1.200% más que en el mismo periodo del año anterior, según el folleto de su salida a bolsa. La compañía registró unas pérdidas netas de 104.000 millones de dólares durante ese periodo de nueve meses, aunque la mayor parte se debió a la variación del valor razonable de los pagarés convertibles y los pasivos por derivados. En el mismo periodo del 2025, Anthropic perdió 25.100 millones de dólares.

stories.headline: Democrats nominate Hakeem Jeffries for House speaker after midterm gains

sources.body:
Democrats in the US House of Representatives officially nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be Speaker, setting him on the path to become the first black lawmaker to lead the chamber.

The House will elect its new Speaker on 3 January, when the next term begins and Democrats will be in the majority.

His election to the powerful position - the Speaker is in line to succeed the president after the vice-president - is widely expected. Should he win, Jeffries will preside over his party's largest House majority in years and benefit from the Senate also being under Democrats' control.

Jeffries told reporters after the vote that the nomination was "a high honour and a distinct privilege".

As of Wednesday, Democrats will hold at least 257 seats in the House next year, which is well beyond the 218 needed for a majority. Seven races from the recent midterm elections are still uncalled.

Jeffries, who represents a district in New York, was re-elected as the party leader in a 251-11 closed-door vote on Wednesday. He has served as minority leader since 2023.

The Congressional Black Caucus, currently made up of only Democratic House members, noted the potential history-making moment when Jeffries takes the helm of the House.

"The American people, largely driven by turnout among Black communities, particularly across the south, have trusted us to make Washington work for them," said the committee's chair, Yvette Clarke, in a statement. "Now, it is our charge and responsibility to do all we can to deliver on their faith."

Despite overwhelming support in Wednesday's vote , Jeffries faced a handful of holdouts from new members in the party's left wing, who have said the party's sweeping victory in the midterm elections is a sign voters want change.

"While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes in this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of our leadership," seven incoming lawmakers, including fellow New Yorkers Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, said in a statement.

All congressional Democrats are gearing up for clashes with the White House once they officially take control in January.

President Donald Trump, a Republican, has signalled a willingness to work with Democrats on some issues, but has also pledged to use his veto power to reject legislation he does not like.

Trump's opposition could make it hard for Democrats to deliver on their campaign promises to address affordability and pass other reforms.

At a news conference following the vote on Wednesday, Jeffries pledged that House Democrats would "fight to lower the high costs of groceries and gas and housing", and "make healthcare affordable for every single American".

Though the party will have a large enough majority to weather defections on must-pass legislation, Jeffries will still have to navigate internal ideological divisions that have grown particularly sharp over US support of Israel and Americans' rising healthcare costs .
sources.headline: Democrats nominate Hakeem Jeffries to be US Speaker of the House

sources.body: Hakeem Jeffries is on the cusp of becoming the first Black speaker of the US House of Representatives after Democrats elected him their leader Wednesday following a sweeping midterm election triumph. sources.body:
The New York congressman is nominated after Democrats gained control of Congress in this month’s midterm elections.

Washington, DC, United States – Hakeem Jeffries has become the first Black lawmaker officially nominated for speaker of the US House of Representatives, marking a milestone in the country’s political history.

In a closed-door vote on Wednesday, the 56-year-old New York congressman secured his party’s nomination for the post just weeks after Democrats scored sweeping victories in the midterm elections, reclaiming control of both chambers of the US Congress.

After voting concluded, Jeffries took to social media to thank his fellow Democrats for their support.

“Together, we will deliver bold change. And make a big difference in the lives of the American people!” he wrote in a post on X.

Amid growing dissent among progressives over his leadership, Jeffries confirmed plans to force members of his party to take a recorded vote on Wednesday.

Some of those members, most of whom were elected this month, declined to say whether they would support Jeffries. Several said they wanted a leader who would support bold, populist policies they had campaigned on.

One of the most vocal holdouts, Congressman-elect Don Leonard of Ohio, refused to commit to Jeffries unless he received guarantees on some progressive priorities, including halting US military aid to Israel and reforming campaign finance standards set by the Supreme Court case Citizens United.

“Unless Speaker Jeffries is willing to commit to enforcing our nation’s laws like the Leahy Law against Israeli genocide in Gaza, unless the speaker is willing to get to the heart of this crisis, which is Citizens United, he will not have my vote,” the Ohio Democrat said in a video posted to social media.

Jeffries has received pushback within some Democratic circles over his record on Israel and ties to pro-Israel lobbying groups, like AIPAC, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. During an interview with The Atlantic magazine on Tuesday, Jeffries addressed some of that criticism, calling for “dramatic change” in the Middle East and a two-state solution.

Despite some opposition in Wednesday’s vote, Jeffries received overwhelming support from the House Democratic Caucus with 251 members voting to back his candidacy. Only 11 members opposed it.

Seven of those who voted against Jeffries included newly-elected Democrats Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York, Adam Hamawy of New Jersey, Melat Kiros of Colorado, Donavan McKinney of Michigan, Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania and Claire Valdez of New York.

Those members released a statement, which was shared with Al Jazeera, detailing their opposition they said was over failure to receive commitments from Jeffries on policies like “Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics or ending the genocide in Gaza”.

“While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership”, the soon-to-be lawmakers wrote. “Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no”.

stories.headline: Democrats explore immigration deal with Trump despite Stephen Miller’s elevation

sources.body: In the days before the midterm election, Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas) felt confident that a blue wave could open the door to immigration reform. Cuellar was so bullish that he reached out to acting Immigration and Customs Enforcement director David Venturella and the Customs and Border Protection commissioner Rodney Scott to feel out areas of “common ground,” he said in an interview. Now Cuellar is one of several moderate Democrats angling to strike a deal with the White House, especially on reining in ICE officers and creating legal pathways to citizenship for some immigrants. They’re undeterred by President Donald Trump’s elevation of immigration hardliner Stephen Miller to chief of staff. And they’re buoyed by Trump’s recent admission that his deportations policy was “too tough.” Several of these Democrats have already placed calls to Trump and DHS secretary Markwayne Mullin to express a willingness to work together. Cuellar said he reached back out to Venturella and Scott after the election to try to schedule meetings. “If the president, as the president of the United States, makes a decision — and not a chief of staff — we can get the job done,” Cuellar said in an interview. “I’m sure we’re going to find a lot of differences, but if we sit down, we can definitely resolve them.” It’ll be a tough road: Securing buy-in from the White House becomes undoubtedly more complicated with Miller, a champion of the administration’s aggressive deportation push. Republicans in Congress have largely been willing to defer to the president on the issue. And Democratic leaders have questioned Trump’s sincerity and said they have no interest in working with Miller. The possibility will become even more tenuous once Democrats begin investigating the Trump administration, including the president’s immigration enforcement agencies. CBP and ICE did not respond to requests for comment. Neither did Democratic leaders Sen. Chuck Schumer and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries. Democrats like Cuellar, Sen.-elects James Talarico of Texas and Annie Andrews of South Carolina are aware of all of those hurdles. But they’re betting the midterms have created an opening for serious talks: Latino voters across the country swung hard back toward Democrats this cycle, and more and more Republicans are recognizing that their immigration agenda hurt them politically. Talarico and Andrews have publicly expressed interest in working with the president on immigration, and both ran on platforms that emphasized creating paths to citizenship for undocumented immigrants. “I’m ready to work with President Trump to fix this broken immigration system,” Talarico said in a statement. Inside the White House, there’s a recognition that the president will proceed however he so chooses, regardless of who the chief of staff is. Trump is accessible to outside voices — journalists, business leaders and lawmakers regularly call him directly — and often poses policy questions to aides and allies as he decides which direction he will go. “Everybody’s like, ‘Well, it’s never going to happen with Stephen Miller.’ Look, Donald Trump’s the president. I don’t care if Stephen Miller’s the chief of staff or Susie Wiles or John Kelly or whoever the chief of staff might be,” said a person close to the White House, granted anonymity to speak about the internal dynamic. For Democrats, there’s a real political incentive to getting a deal done ahead of a critical 2028 presidential election — especially as the party seeks to win back voter trust on immigration and border security, policy areas that spelled doom for them in 2024. “You have these Democrats who flip red states, and it’s also to their self-interest, right? Not just to do rhetoric, and go big or go home, but actually come to the middle with the president, with the Republicans. Because if not, I think that the big lesson this election is, Hispanic voters are gonna flip back ... if they don’t see Democrats delivering anything the next two years,” said Rebecca Shi, the executive director of ABIC, a coalition of pro-immigration reform business executives. She added that there’s a lesson for Republicans, too, if they don’t come to the table: “They will lose the White House.” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis touted Trump’s immigration accomplishments, including border security, a drop in crime and the creation of the Homeland Security Task Force and said the president’s “strong immigration policy remains unchanged.” She said Democrats should work alongside Trump to “keep our southern border secure, remove dangerous illegal criminals from our communities, and stop the illicit trafficking of lethal drugs.” Democrats welcomed the president’s remarks on 60 Minutes on Sunday, when he said he was open to legal pathways for some unauthorized immigrants who haven’t committed crimes and are working and contributing to the economy. Mullin also floated an openness to a bipartisan immigration overhaul involving DACA, which could provide permanent legal status to some undocumented immigrants who arrived in the U.S. as children, even as he — and the president — have insisted that any proposal wouldn’t include amnesty. In a sign that Democrats have learned the lessons of the Biden administration , many of them are eager to pair reforms with border security measures. Cuellar, who will chair the Homeland Security Appropriations subcommittee in the next conference, has long suggested including guardrails on ICE in the next funding bill, such as requiring judicial warrants, rolling out body camera usage and restoring “sensitive locations” such as churches and schools as off-limits. Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.), another Democrat who has expressed interest in working with the Trump administration, said that beyond “talk,” it would help to see some smaller concrete policy shifts from the White House to affirm that Trump is, in fact, open to changes to the immigration system. “The way to do that is to have some reforms already at ICE — whether it’s shutting down these detention centers, giving certain level of protections, whether to veterans, so they don't get deported, to maybe parents of U.S. citizens, they don’t get deported — something to show that, you know, it's not just talk, this isn’t going to be a policy led by Stephen Miller,” he said. But Miller remains a bogeyman for Democrats, someone they view as responsible for the president’s most extreme immigration policies. As chief of staff, he can ensure he’s one of the last people in the president’s ear — and that the White House doesn’t bend to what he sees as unrealistic Democratic demands. “The reason why they wouldn’t do an amnesty deal, I believe, is because it would be the ultimate and most public contradiction of the central thesis of this entire political program as it was sold to voters,” said Mike Howell, president of the Oversight Project and a member of the Mass Deportation Coalition. “It would be the end of the America First coalition as it currently exists.” Democrats' distrust of Miller will also make it challenging for them to align on any potential deal with the White House. “Stephen Miller is the mastermind and architect of terror, and death, and illegality in this country, and he is not anyone who even understands truthfully what immigration policy should look like,” said Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-Calif). “No deals, man. No deals,” she added. The White House pointed to Miller’s experience on the Hill as a valuable asset. White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers said unlike Democrats “who refused to work with the President and blocked many of his popular policies, Stephen Miller has a track record of spearheading bipartisan efforts: public safety reform, making our cities such as Washington, D.C. and Memphis safe again, drug pricing transparency, and unleashing a nuclear energy renaissance.” Lawmakers are waiting for the president to make the first move. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, who will continue to lead his fellow Republicans when Democrats retake control of the Senate this January, told reporters after the election that “if there's something he wants to do there, we can have that conversation.” “There are always some landmines, which is why in the past the wheels have kind of come off, despite some really good efforts at trying to find a landing spot. But yeah we're open to something he wants to propose,” Thune added. Jordain Carney contributed to this report.
sources.headline: Democrats see an immigration opening despite Stephen Miller’s rise

sources.body: Oklahoma’s Republican governor warned against populist economic ideas gaining popularity, as he called for fellow Republicans to reject socialism and embrace free markets and an “ownership economy.” “A socialist or a populist economy is something that is not American,” Gov. Kevin Stitt said in an interview on Wednesday at the POLITICO Pub, on the sidelines of the National Governors Association's New Governors Leadership Forum in Deer Valley, Utah. “We should all be concerned about the amount of people that think that socialism is the answer.” When asked if he was concerned about socialist tendencies on the right, Stitt criticized fellow Republicans who have called for data center moratoriums.. “When you start dictating … you see some people from the far right saying, ‘Well, we don’t want data centers. We don’t want that,’” Stitt said. “When did we become a party that if you follow all the rules, you follow the permitting, the clean water, the clean air, and you own your own land, that we allow the government to tell you what you can do on that property?” the Oklahoma governor asked. “That is what I'm talking about, that we need to be very, very careful about.” Stitt also called on President Donald Trump to use his final two years in the White House to push for bipartisan immigration reform — his latest remarks on the topic. “We need to have a strong border. We need to know who is coming into our country. We need to vet those people,” Stitt told POLITICO’s Samuel Benson. “He can lead on this, he can fix this immigration policy. “To me, we are overthinking it,” Stitt added. “It is as simple as: If an employer is vouching for an employee, the state governors should be able to issue that workforce permit. Period, end of story.” Stitt described Trump as a “business person” who “understands the need for a workforce.” But he blamed Congress and other interests in Washington for standing in the way of reform. “It's not that complicated. But the problem is Washington, D.C., each side thinks they're winning on it. They raise money off of it. They politic off of it. They try to crush the other side over these issues instead of fixing it for the American people,” Stitt said. “That's why you saw this huge swing in the midterms.”
sources.headline: Oklahoma GOP governor warns of growing socialist tendencies on the right

sources.body:
La Diputación Permanente del Congreso ha convalidado este miércoles los siete últimos reales decretos-leyes aprobados por el Consejo de Ministros en el último mes, a raíz de la convocatoria electoral y la disolución de las Cortes. Entre otras, han salido adelante ayudas para las víctimas del accidente de tren de Urda (Toledo) y otras de apoyo financiero para Ceuta y para paliar los efectos de la dana Adam; medidas para reforzar la seguridad en el transporte ferroviario y mejorar las condiciones de su plantilla; e iniciativas de calado social que amplían la protección a las familias monoparentales y mejoran el sistema de dependencia.

Los siete decretos han salido adelante con la mayoría absoluta del órgano. Los partidos del Gobierno -PSOE y Sumar-, así como sus socios de investidura -ERC, EH Bildu, PNV y Podemos- han votado a favor de todos ellos. También lo ha hecho el PP , mientras que Junts se ha abstenido en el relativo a la protección de las familias monoparentales y Vox solo ha dado su apoyo al decreto de ayudas a las víctimas del accidente ferroviario.

En esta ocasión, no ha sido decisivo el voto del PNV, algo que sí ocurrió el pasado jueves en las votaciones sobre los decretos de vivienda. Los nacionalistas vascos respaldaron uno de los textos , el que prohíbe los desahucios, y permitieron su convalidación. En el otro, que hacía indefinidos los alquileres, votaron en contra junto a PP, Vox y Junts, y el decreto quedó derogado.

La Diputación Permanente del Congreso, el único órgano parlamentario que permanece activo tras la disolución de las Cortes, podrá reunirse la próxima semana por última vez antes de las elecciones generales del 29 de noviembre. Tras los comicios, el Gobierno quedará en funciones hasta que tome posesión el nuevo Ejecutivo, tal como establece el artículo 101 de la Constitución.

Uno de los momentos más broncos de la jornada ha coincidido con el debate del decreto de ayudas a Ceuta, con el que se destinan 45,32 millones de euros en subvenciones directas a la ciudad autónoma para financiar las actuaciones tras la llegada masiva de migrantes a finales de julio .

El ministro de Política Territorial y Memoria Democrática, Ángel Víctor Torres, ha sido el encargado de defender la iniciativa, asegurando que "se está recuperando la normalidad" en la ciudad y que todos los asentamientos están desalojados y ya no hay grupos pernoctando. Además, ha avanzado que este miércoles comienzan las obras de ampliación del espigón y del obstáculo flotante, que pasará a tener más de medio kilómetro.

Las críticas no han tardado en llegar desde la oposición. La diputada del PP Sofía Acedo Reyes ha advertido al Ejecutivo de que la ciudad solo "empezará a recuperar la normalidad el día que salgan todos los que invadieron la ciudad el 30 y 31 de julio" y lo ha acusado de "abandonar" a los ceutíes. Mientras que Vox ve la "invasión" de Ceuta motivo de "una declaración de guerra" y ha reclamado la "defensa permanente" del Ejército y una "acción penal" contra el Gobierno.

sources.headline: El Congreso aprueba siete decretos sociales con un amplísimo respaldo pero entre críticas de campaña

sources.body:
La ministra de Inclusión, Seguridad Social y Migraciones, Elma Saiz, conversa con el vicepresidente primero, Carlos Cuerpo 

Con la campaña electoral en marcha y el Gobierno ha aprovechado la Diputación Permanente del Congreso para desplegar una nueva batería de medidas sociales. En un contexto marcado por los sondeos desfavorables para el bloque progresista, el órgano parlamentario ha convalidado este miércoles siete decretos ley que abarcan desde la reforma del sistema de dependencia hasta las ayudas por la dana, pasando por el refuerzo ferroviario y las indemnizaciones a las víctimas del accidente de Urda. Una ofensiva legislativa que ha vuelto a enfrentar al Ejecutivo con PP y Vox, que han denunciado el uso electoral de las instituciones.

El paquete normativo aprobado abarca un amplio abanico de actuaciones que incluye desde las ayudas para reparar los efectos de la crisis migratoria registrada en Ceuta este verano hasta las subvenciones para paliar los daños causados por las inundaciones de la dana Adam los pasados 17 y 19 de octubre, pasando por mejoras en el sistema de la Seguridad Social, el refuerzo de la red ferroviaria tras los últimos siniestros o la ampliación de la protección a las familias numerosas y monomarentales.

El marcado ha dibujado un apoyo casi unánime, con la única excepción de Vox, a seis de los siete decretos. La formación de extrema derecha sí se ha sumado al consenso para aprobar por unanimidad, con los votos favorables de los 69 diputados presentes, el decreto que articula las subvenciones, ayudas e indemnizaciones destinadas a las familias de las 69 víctimas mortales y a los heridos en el siniestro ferroviario de Urda.

Los ministros que han defendido las iniciativas han justificado el recurso a la legislación de urgencia por la trascendencia de las medidas y la necesidad de avanzar en derechos sociales que afectan a millones de ciudadanos, sin esperar a la constitución de las nuevas Cámaras. La oposición, por el contrario, ha cuestionado que el Ejecutivo recurra a esta fórmula excepcional con las Cortes disueltas y a las puertas de las elecciones.

Las palabras más gruesas han llegado de la mano del cabeza de lista de Vox por Ciudad Real, Ricardo Chamorro, quien ha intervenido durante el debate del decreto sobre la dana Adam, defendido por el ministro de Política Territorial y Memoria Democrática, Ángel Víctor Torres. Chamorro ha tachado al PSOE de ser “amoral desde el punto de vista electoral” y ha censurado que, con el Parlamento disuelto, acudan “ministro tras ministro a exhibir partidas millonarias y a presentar las bondades de su Gobierno a diez días de las elecciones”.

El diputado de Vox ha denunciado la “doble vara de medir” de los socialistas, a quienes ha reprochado que acudan de forma constante ante la Junta Electoral para denunciar a otras formaciones por publicitar su gestión mientras convierten una sesión de diez horas en el Congreso en “un mitin electoral de Pedro Sánchez”. Chamorro también ha cuestionado las ayudas aprobadas, que ha considerado insuficientes y tardías, y ha acusado al Ejecutivo de una gestión marcada, a su juicio, por la “corrupción y negligencia”.
sources.headline: El Congreso convalida siete decretos sociales entre acusaciones de electoralismo del PP y Vox

stories.headline: Spain outlines plan for fully renewable electricity by 2040 and fossil fuel phaseout by 2050

sources.body:
Aerogeneradores, en una imagen de archivo. / AUDAX RENOVABLES

España se ha comprometido en la cumbre del clima de Antalya (COP31) a sumarse a la lista de países que, en su afán por avanzar en la acción climática global, desarrollarán un plan estatal propio para dejar atrás los combustibles fósiles . Según ha podido saber este diario a partir de fuentes conocedoras del texto, la estrategia aspira a desplegar medidas a corto plazo con el objetivo final de llegar a 2040 con un 100% de electricidad generada a partir de energías renovables y a 2050 con una economía completamente descarbonizada y libre de petróleo, gas y carbón . El plan, elaborado por el actual Gobierno, plantea poner en marcha una transformación transversal que afectará desde los edificios residenciales hasta el sector de los servicios, el mundo agrícola y la movilidad urbana y que, finalmente, también se extenderá a sectores más difíciles de transformar como la industria y el transporte pesado.

La iniciativa, alineada con el Plan Nacional Integrado de Energía y Clima (PNIEC) y la Ley de Cambio Climático, establece un ambicioso calendario para acelerar el abandono de los combustibles fósiles. De cara a 2030, contempla que el apoyo público en materia energética se destine exclusivamente a las energías renovables, con el objetivo de alcanzar una cuota del 81% de generación eléctrica renovable y del 48% de renovables en el consumo final de energía . Para ello, la estrategia apuesta por intensificar la electrificación de la economía y reducir progresivamente la dependencia del petróleo, el gas y el carbón.

Siguiendo en esta línea, para 2040 se espera avanzar aún más en la descarbonización y dar prioridad a la eliminación de combustibles fósiles en edificios residenciales, servicios, sector primario y movilidad urbana. Con todo esto, se espera lograr un sistema eléctrico 100 % renovable y una reducción del 90 % de las emisiones netas respecto a 1990.

El objetivo último de la hoja de ruta, en línea con los compromisos internacionales de lucha contra el cambio climático, es que España complete en 2050 el abandono definitivo de los combustibles fósiles . Para alcanzar esta meta, según explican fuentes cercanas a la elaboración del documento, la estrategia contempla extender la descarbonización a todos los usos de la energía, más allá de la generación eléctrica. Esto implica sustituir progresivamente el petróleo, el gas y el carbón no solo en los hogares y los servicios, sino también en aquellos sectores donde la transición resulta más compleja, como la industria y el transporte pesado, que requieren alternativas tecnológicas específicas. El horizonte es avanzar hacia una economía plenamente descarbonizada en la que las necesidades energéticas del país puedan cubrirse sin recurrir a los combustibles fósiles y solo mediante renovables.

La "hoja de ruta española" para abandonar los combustibles fósiles se ha diseñado en torno a seis ejes estratégicos. El primero es la eficiencia energética , orientada a reducir la demanda y optimizar el consumo de energía. El segundo es la electrificación , que busca sustituir progresivamente los combustibles fósiles por electricidad de origen renovable. El tercero contempla el despliegue de energías renovables para garantizar un suministro limpio y competitivo. El cuarto es la innovación tecnológica , clave para desarrollar soluciones como el hidrógeno verde y los combustibles avanzados en sectores difíciles de electrificar.
sources.headline: España traza un plan para alcanzar la electricidad 100% renovable en 2040 y dejar atrás el petróleo y el gas en 2050

stories.headline: Barcelona releases five plots for 410 affordable rental homes

sources.body:
L’ Ajuntament de Barcelona cedeix a a la societat mixta Habitatge Metròpolis Barcelona (HMB) cinc solars per a la construcció de 410 pisos per a lloguer assequible. La Comissió de Presidència, Seguretat i Règim Interior d’aquest dimecres n’ha aprovat definitivament la cessió.

Els solars se cediran en dret de superfície a l’HMB per un període de 75 anys i, en cap moment, el sòl perdrà la titularitat municipal. Dos dels solars estan ubicats al districte de Sants-Montjuïc i els altres tres a Sant Martí .

L’HMB treballa ja en els projectes d’aquestes promocions de manera que la previsió és que el darrer trimestre del 2026 puguin iniciar-se les obres d’una de les promocions, la del carrer dels Ferrocarrils Catalans. El primer trimestre del 2027 està previst que s’iniciïn les promocions dels carrers de Zamora, del Marroc i de Miquel Porter i Moix, mentre que la promoció de carrer de Tànger està previst que s’iniciï el primer trimestre de 2028.

Aquesta és la segona tongada de solars que Barcelona cedeix a l’HMB. El 2022, a la primera fase, es van cedir quatre solars que actualment es troben en fase d’execució. En total, en la primera fase eren 331 habitatges.

Actualment, estan en fase prèvia d’estudi els sòls a aportar en una tercera fase: tres solars per a tres promocions per a aixecar un total de 528 habitatges.

Habitatge Metròpolis Barcelona es va crear el 2021 com a operador metropolità d’habitatge de lloguer assequible participat en un 50% pel sector públic (25% l’AMB i 25% l’Ajuntament de Barcelona) i privat NICRent Residencial SL en un altre 50 %. L’operador es va constituir per promoure fins a 4.500 habitatges de lloguer assequible.

Tots els habitatges que promoguts per Habitatge Metròpolis Barcelona, es destinaran al lloguer assequible i tindran la qualificació de protegits de manera permanent per tal d’evitar una eventual desprotecció i pèrdua d’habitatges assequibles.

El tinent d’alcaldia de l’àrea econòmica, Jordi Valls, ha remarcat la necessitat de col·laborar amb el sector privat i financer per construir habitatge. “Si volem construir el volum d’habitatge que requereix construir Barcelona i Catalunya necessitem que el sector financer, que el sector privat ens pugui acompanyar”, ha argumentat Valls, que ha subratllat que el gran repte no és només comprar habitatge, sinó sobretot crear sòl. També ha destacat que aquesta operació garanteix que el solar sempre serà públic i que l’habitatge serà sempre protegit, ha recollit l’ACN .
sources.headline: L’Ajuntament cedeix cinc solars per a la construcció de 410 pisos per a lloguer assequible

sources.body:
De un total de 4.500 en el área metropolitana

Edificio de pisos en alquiler en la ciudad de Barcelona / Elisenda Pons / EPC

Barcelona levantará unos 410 pisos de protección oficial destinados al alquiler en cinco solares municipales , tras haber aprobado este miércoles por la mañana la Comisión de Ecología, Urbanismo, Movilidad y Vivienda la constitución de los derechos reales de superficie de las fincas a la sociedad mixta Habitatge Metròpoli Barcelona (HMB). Los solares están situados en los distritos de Sant Martí y de Sants-Montjuïc."Si queremos construir el volumen de vivienda que requieren Barcelona y Catalunya, necesitamos que el sector financiero nos pueda acompañar ", ha declarado el sexto teniente de Alcaldía del Ayuntamiento de Barcelona, Jordi Valls , quien considera que "el gran reto es crear suelo" para poder sumar vivienda. Los pisos se encuentran en las calles de Miquel Porter i Moix (89 viviendas), Tànger (72), Zamora (93), Marroc (96) y Ferrocarrils Catalans (60).

El edil socialista ha detallado que se trata de la segunda fase de un proyecto que contempla levantar unas 4.500 viviendas ; entre 2.000 y 2.500 de las cuales en la ciudad de Barcelona y, el resto, en el resto de los municipios del área metropolitana. La cesión será por 75 años , con un cánon de 100 euros al año por vivienda. En una primera fase, ha detallado Valls, en el año 2022 se cedieron cuatro solares para construir unas 330 viviendas en los ámbitos de la Marina de Prat Vermell, en la Sagrera y en las casernas de Sant Andreu. Habitatge Metròpoli Barcelona es una sociedad mixta publicoprivada , y está dedicada a la promoción y gestión de viviendas de alquiler asequible en el área metropolitana de Barcelona.

Constituida en 2021, HMB está participada al 50% por capital público (a medias entre el Ayuntamiento y el AMB) y al 50% por capital privado a través de la sociedad Nicrent Residencial, integrada a su vez por las promotoras privadas Cevasa y Neinor Homes. "Este gobierno siempre ha dicho que es absolutamente necesario construir y regular, pero cuando hablamos de construir es necesario hacerlo mediante alianzas", ha señalado Valls, que asimismo ha adelantado que "se está trabajando para seguir constituyendo derechos de superficie para la construcción de 528 viviendas más ". Las viviendas promovidas por HMB tendrán la calificación de protegidas de manera permanente, señala el gobierno municipal, para evitar así "una eventual desprotección y pérdida de vivienda asequible".

La propuesta ha tirado adelante con los votos favorables del PSC, Junts, Barcelona en Comú y Vox; y la abstención de ERC y PP . El concejal Damià Calvet (Junts) ha declarado que "comparten la finalidad de construir vivienda de protección oficial en alquiler, manteniendo la titularidad pública del suelo" y ha destacado también la importancia de la colaboración público-privada, como "parte de la solución al acceso a la vivienda". Por su parte, la concejala de los Comuns Lucía Martín también ha celebrado el proyecto, que ha recordado fue impulsado por su grupo en el ámbito del Àrea Metropolitana de Barcelona (AMB), aunque ha afeado al gobierno municipal que este "llega tarde", ya que el calendario contemplaba que, a estas alturas, la primera promoción ya estuviese finalizada.
